claims.text: Transient chemical short-range order develops in multi-element near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles during exposure to 473–1923 K in reactive or inert atmospheres.
Chemical short-range order reduces interdiffusion kinetics.
Chemical short-range order reduces phase-separation kinetics.
The resulting kinetic suppression governs structural and chemical stability during extended thermal cycling.
Short-range ordering imposes kinetic barriers on phase separation, grain coarsening, and surface segregation.
Local compositional rearrangements and partial ordering of dissimilar atoms reduce atomic mobility.
High mixing or configurational entropy stabilizes a single-phase solid solution against intermetallic formation.
Near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles will show delayed or suppressed phase separation relative to monometallic or binary/ternary reference nanoparticles.
Near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles will undergo less grain growth than the reference nanoparticles during repeated thermal cycling.
Near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles will retain greater compositional uniformity than the reference nanoparticles after repeated thermal cycling.
Monometallic or simpler multicomponent reference materials typically transform or coarsen earlier under comparable conditions.
The proposed stabilization mechanism applies primarily to initially single-phase, minimally segregated, near-equiatomic nanoparticles smaller than approximately 20 nm.
The proposed stabilization mechanism remains effective up to approximately 1900 K.
Above approximately 1900 K, entropy or local ordering may no longer suppress diffusion-limited coarsening or phase separation.
Related multicomponent alloys have shown persistent solid-solution character or high thermal stability.
Entropy-stabilized high-entropy alloys can nevertheless undergo irreversible polymorphic transformations under suitable pressure and temperature conditions.

contradictions.description: The intervention specifies cycling from about 300 to 1923 K, whereas the conditions specify cycles from 473 to 1923 K.

The mechanism is bounded to about 1900 K, but the experiment extends to 1923 K and treats degradation at or below approximately 1923 K as falsifying the mechanism, thereby including temperatures outside its stated validity range.
